a1-sein-haben.title: Sein and Haben: To Be and To Have
a1-sein-haben.pattern: ich bin/habe, du bist/hast, er ist/hat, wir sind/haben, ihr seid/habt, sie sind/haben
a1-sein-haben.explanation: "Sein" (to be) and "haben" (to have) are the two most important verbs in German and both are irregular: ich bin/habe, du bist/hast, er/sie/es ist/hat, wir sind/haben, ihr seid/habt, sie/Sie sind/haben. You'll use them constantly — for descriptions, ages, and forming other tenses later on.
a1-sein-haben.fact: German has a formal "you" (Sie, always capitalized) used with strangers, elders, and in professional settings, separate from the informal "du". "Sie sind" (formal you are) looks identical to "sie sind" (they are) in writing except for the capital letter — context and capitalization both matter.

dialogue.native: Ich heiße Anna. Und ich bin Studentin.
dialogue.en: My name is Anna. And I am a student.

a1-present-regular.title: Present Tense: Regular Verbs
a1-present-regular.pattern: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en
a1-present-regular.explanation: Most German verbs are regular and follow one pattern in the present tense: take the infinitive (e.g. "spielen", to play), drop "-en", and add: -e/-st/-t/-en/-t/-en. "Ich spiele" (I play), "du spielst" (you play), "er spielt" (he plays), "wir spielen" (we play). This single pattern covers the vast majority of German verbs.
a1-present-regular.fact: German has only ONE present tense form where English has two — "ich spiele" translates both "I play" and "I am playing". There's no separate progressive/continuous form in standard German, so context tells you which English translation fits.

dialogue.en: What are you doing right now?

dialogue.native: Ich lerne Deutsch und höre Musik.
dialogue.en: I'm learning German and listening to music.

a1-articles-gender.title: Der, Die, Das: Gender and Articles
a1-articles-gender.explanation: Every German noun has one of three genders — masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das) — and this determines the article: "der Mann" (the man), "die Frau" (the woman), "das Kind" (the child). The indefinite article follows the same pattern: "ein Mann", "eine Frau", "ein Kind". German nouns are ALWAYS capitalized, no matter where they appear in a sentence.
a1-articles-gender.fact: Gender is mostly unpredictable and must be memorized with each new noun — always learn a noun together with its article ("die Tasche", not just "Tasche"). A few endings are reliable hints: words ending in -chen or -lein are always neuter (das Mädchen), words ending in -heit, -keit, -ung, or -schaft are always feminine (die Freundschaft).

dialogue.native: Ist das ein Buch oder eine Zeitschrift?

a1-akkusativ.title: Akkusativ: The Direct Object Case
a1-akkusativ.pattern: der → den, ein → einen (masc. only) · die/eine, das/ein stay the same
a1-akkusativ.explanation: The Akkusativ case marks the direct object of a sentence — the thing directly receiving the action. Only the MASCULINE article changes: "der" → "den", "ein" → "einen". Feminine and neuter articles look identical to Nominativ: "Ich sehe den Mann" (I see the man) but "Ich sehe die Frau" / "Ich sehe das Kind" (unchanged). This is the first of German's four cases you'll learn — and the easiest, since only one gender changes.
a1-akkusativ.fact: A small set of common prepositions ALWAYS take the Akkusativ, no matter the context: "für" (for), "durch" (through), "ohne" (without), "gegen" (against), "um" (around) — memorize these together as "für durch ohne gegen um", a classic learner's mnemonic.

dialogue.native: Hier, ich habe einen für dich.
dialogue.en: Here, I have one for you.

a1-negation-wordorder.title: Negation with Nicht/Kein, and Verb-Second Word Order
a1-negation-wordorder.pattern: kein negates a noun (kein Buch) · nicht negates everything else · verb is always position 2
a1-negation-wordorder.explanation: German has two negation words: "kein" (no/not a) negates a noun that would otherwise take "ein" or no article: "Ich habe kein Auto" (I don't have a car). "Nicht" negates verbs, adjectives, and definite-article nouns: "Ich verstehe das nicht" (I don't understand that). German word order is famously strict about one rule: the CONJUGATED verb always sits in position 2 of a normal statement, even if something other than the subject starts the sentence: "Heute arbeite ich nicht" (Today I'm not working — verb still second, subject moves after it).
a1-negation-wordorder.fact: This verb-second (V2) rule is unlike English, where word order is more flexible — in German, whatever element you choose to emphasize by placing first (a time expression, a direct object, etc.) simply pushes the subject after the verb, but the verb itself never moves from position 2 in a main clause.

dialogue.native: Nein, heute arbeite ich nicht. Ich habe keine Zeit für Meetings.
dialogue.en: No, I'm not working today. I have no time for meetings.

a1-w-questions.title: W-Questions: Wer, Was, Wo, Wann, Warum, Wie
a1-w-questions.explanation: German question words all start with W (like English "wh-" words): "wer" (who), "was" (what), "wo" (where), "wann" (when), "warum" (why), "wie" (how), "wie viel/wie viele" (how much/many). Like statements, the conjugated verb comes right after the question word, in position 2: "Wo wohnst du?" (Where do you live?), "Was machst du?" (What are you doing?).
a1-w-questions.fact: "Wo" (where, as in a fixed location) and "wohin" (where to, as in a direction) are genuinely different words in German — "Wo bist du?" (Where are you?) versus "Wohin gehst du?" (Where are you going [to]?) — mixing them up is a very common learner error.

dialogue.native: Ich war zu Hause. Warum fragst du?
dialogue.en: I was at home. Why do you ask?

a1-modal-verbs.title: Modal Verbs: Können, Müssen, Wollen, Möchten, Dürfen
a1-modal-verbs.pattern: modal (conjugated, position 2) + ... + infinitive (sent to the end)
a1-modal-verbs.explanation: Modal verbs express ability, necessity, desire, or permission: "können" (can/to be able to), "müssen" (must/have to), "wollen" (to want to), "möchten" (would like to, more polite than wollen), "dürfen" (may/to be allowed to). The modal verb is conjugated and sits in position 2, while the main action verb goes to the very end of the sentence as a plain infinitive: "Ich kann gut Deutsch sprechen" (I can speak German well).
a1-modal-verbs.fact: Modal verbs (except "möchten" and "sollen") have irregular, vowel-changing forms in the singular that don't follow the regular pattern: "ich kann/muss/will", "du kannst/musst/willst", "er kann/muss/will" — notice there's no -t ending on "er/sie/es" the way regular verbs have, a genuine irregularity to memorize.

dialogue.native: Kannst du mir helfen? Ich muss diese Aufgabe fertig machen.

dialogue.en: Sure, I would love to help you.

a1-numbers-time.title: Numbers, Time, and Dates
a1-numbers-time.pattern: eins, zwei, drei... · Es ist ... Uhr · am + [day/date]
a1-numbers-time.explanation: German numbers are mostly regular: eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn — and compound numbers reverse the order compared to English: "einundzwanzig" is literally "one-and-twenty" (21). Telling time uses "Es ist ... Uhr": "Es ist drei Uhr" (It's three o'clock). Days and dates use "am": "am Montag" (on Monday), "am ersten Mai" (on the first of May).
a1-numbers-time.fact: In casual spoken German, half-hours are expressed relative to the UPCOMING hour, not the previous one — "halb drei" means "half TO three" (2:30), not "half past two" as an English speaker might assume at first glance — a common source of confusion for beginners.

dialogue.native: Es ist halb drei. Wir treffen uns um vier.
dialogue.en: It's half past two. We're meeting at four.

a1-plurals.title: Plural Formation: No Single Rule
a1-plurals.pattern: -e, -er, -(e)n, -s, or no change — each noun's plural must be learned individually
a1-plurals.explanation: Unlike English's reliable "-s", German plurals form in several different ways depending on the noun, often with an added umlaut: "der Tisch" → "die Tische" (-e), "das Kind" → "die Kinder" (-er), "die Frau" → "die Frauen" (-en), "das Auto" → "die Autos" (-s, common for loanwords), or occasionally no change at all ("der Lehrer" → "die Lehrer"). There is no shortcut — each noun's plural is learned individually, alongside its gender.
a1-plurals.fact: Every plural noun, regardless of the original gender, takes "die" as its article: "der Mann" → "die Männer", "das Kind" → "die Kinder" — gender distinctions disappear entirely in the plural, which is one small mercy in an otherwise irregular system.
